articleText:
[Hacker News — parameter.ai] Labs Close Do the Math: How We Took Over ChatGPT Accounts By bypassing ChatGPT's sandbox and content security policy, our research team was able to take over anyone's account simply by sending them a link. In October 2026, we found a way to turn an ordinary public ChatGPT share into attacker-controlled JavaScript running inside the signed-in session of whoever opened it. An attacker could create a malicious conversation, publish it using ChatGPT's normal sharing feature, and send the link to another user. When the victim opened the share, the payload executed as chatgpt.com with access to the victim's authenticated web session. We confirmed that this code could enumerate the victim's conversation list, retrieve content from a private conversation that had never been shared with the attacker, and send data from that conversation to an external server. The payload was not limited to modifying the page or displaying an alert—it could directly call ChatGPT's authenticated APIs as the victim, essentially allowing us to take over the victim's ChatGPT account. The victim did not need to install an App, join a Project, paste code, or open developer tools. Opening the shared link was the only required action. OpenAI fixed the issue on October 26 and classified the report as P1. The chain started with two features that looked harmless on their own: a graph and an HTML Preview. flowchart TD A["Attacker publishes a ChatGPT conversation"] --> B["Victim opens the public share"] B --> C["HTML Preview crosses into the main chatgpt.com page"] C --> D["JavaScript runs in the victim's signed-in session"] D --> E["Any action on chatgpt.com as the victim:
read private chats and files, change the account"] Technical walkthrough It started with a graph and a Preview The question that started this research was simple: if Preview code was boxed into a different website, what could it still talk to? ChatGPT can turn an HTML code block into a small working webpage using its Preview feature. Since that page may contain arbitrary code, ChatGPT sensibly runs it inside a restricted frame on a different web address. The Preview can run JavaScript, but the browser treats it as a different website, so it cannot directly inspect the signed-in ChatGPT page around it. At first, this isolation appeared to work exactly as intended. Code inside the Preview could not read parent.document , which is the main ChatGPT page. That should have been the end of it. The conversation also contained a normal interactive graph. Behind the scenes, the graph loaded a math library called MathLive. Loading it did more than draw the graph: it also installed a listener in the main ChatGPT page for messages related to MathLive's on-screen keyboard. Browsers call the relevant API postMessage . It is a legitimate way for two frames to exchange information even when the browser prevents them from reading each other's pages. You can think of it as a mail slot: the restricted Preview cannot walk into the main page, but it can still drop a message through the slot. That is safe only if the receiver checks who sent the message. MathLive did not make that check for the setting we were interested in. Its listener accepted a message that changed the virtual keyboard layout, and that layout was allowed to contain HTML. The graph had installed the receiver; the Preview gave us an untrusted sender. Two unrelated features had accidentally created a path across the sandbox. The Preview sent two messages. The first replaced a virtual keyboard layout with our HTML. The second told MathLive to show the keyboard, causing it to render the new layout: top.postMessage({ type: "mathlive#virtual-keyboard-message", action: "update-setting", layouts: [{ label: "Compatibility", layers: [{ id: "compatibility", markup }] }] }, "*"); top.postMessage({ type: "mathlive#virtual-keyboard-message", action: "show", animate: false }, "*"); parameter MathLive recognized the public message type, but its top-level controller used an origin policy of none , which meant it accepted messages from any web address. It also did not require the update-setting message to come from a previously approved window. Anyone who could reach the listener and knew the message format could replace the layout. When the keyboard opened, MathLive joined the supplied layout into an HTML string and assigned it to innerHTML in the real ChatGPT page. A helper named createHTML initially looked like it might sanitize the value. It did not; it marked the string as trusted and passed our HTML through unchanged. This was exciting, but we still did not have JavaScript execution. Script tags inserted through innerHTML do not automatically run. The next step was an iframe using srcdoc , a browser feature that lets an embedded frame carry its HTML directly in an attribute: parameter MathLive inserted this frame into the main ChatGPT document without a sandbox attribute. T --- [Simon Willison — simonwillison.net] How We Took Over ChatGPT Accounts ( via ) Parameter Labs describe an exploit they found against ChatGPT's implementation of the artifacts pattern (OpenAI used to call this "Canvas" but it looks like the latest revision is called HTML previews ), where interactive custom HTML apps are displayed in a sandboxed iframe. It's important that HTML in these stays tightly sandboxed to avoid untrusted code interacting with OpenAI APIs and accessing private data. Parameter found quite a complex attack chain. OpenAI use the MathLive JavaScript library as part of their graph support, and that library includes its own virtual keyboard , which can be triggered in the parent page via postMessage() from the sandboxed iframe. That message receiving code uses innerHTML , so anything that sends a message can add custom HTML to the parent - and there was no mechanism to prevent other sandboxed frames, including HTML preview frames, from calling that method. This meant untrusted code in an iframe could insert HTML, and while innerHTML doesn't directly execute script elements it could be used to inject a new iframe without sandbox restrictions. OpenAI’s CSP rules blocked inline scripts entirely, and only allowed script loading from a handful of domains, but one of those was YouTube - and the YouTube oEmbed endpoint could be used to reflect JavaScript back in a way that executed it. Once the attack had JavaScript execution on ChatGPT, it was trivial to fetch private user data from APIs and exfiltrate it via an image reference. The end result: you could create a ChatGPT share URL which, when visited by another signed-in user, could exfiltrate their private data or take actions on their behalf. OpenAI closed the hole and paid out a $5,000 bug bounty, which I think was a bit cheap for a vulnerability this serious. This is a link post by Simon Willison, posted on 31st October 2026 .
